question_type: two-series arc (midpoint) elasticity between two monthly rows of the IRS collections summary table (total collections vs unemployment insurance)

opus_path.decision: Q = 'Total collections reported by Internal Revenue Service', P = 'Unemployment insurance' column. Midpoint arc elasticity with January as point 1 and March as point 2, keeping the sign, reported to 3 decimals. No issue is pinned, so all vintages must be checked.
INTERNAL REVENUE COLLECTIONS 'Table 1.- Summary by Principal Sources' (in thousands of dollars). The May 1960 issue stops at Feb 1960, so the June 1960 issue or a later one is needed for March.
Pulled the Jan and Mar 1960 rows from every printing from 1960_04 through 1961_03, instead of stopping at the first printing that carries March.

The January row is identical everywhere. The March unemployment-insurance cell has three different values: 8 printings agree, and June 1960 and Sept 1960 each show a different single-digit variant. Took the majority value.

Exact row-sum identity: the four employment/income components sum to the printed subtotal only with the majority value, for both January and March. Also recognized that in some printings the blank Old-age cell migrates to the end of the row, shifting the UI value under the 'Railroad retirement' header.
calc.py computes the midpoint formula. A sensitivity line shows that the June-1960 OCR variant reproduces exactly the value all three GLM arms submitted.

opus_key_moves: Extracted the March UI cell from every printing that carries it, not just the first, and found three competing values
Settled on one value by majority plus an exact row-sum identity computed in code
Recognized the OCR column shift (a blank cell migrating to the row end), so later printings' values could be read under the right header

right_arms_note: No arm was right. All three submitted the identical value, derived from the same OCR-garbled March cell in the June 1960 first printing.
text_vs_mechanism: Mechanism. The prompt arm had the exact verified lesson as text (take the majority, or the value consistent with the printed total), tried to apply it, and failed because it did the deciding sum in its head. The cards arm saw the correct value and explained it away via the column shift. An automatic, code-executed row-sum/majority check, or an all-printings tool that returns the majority value under re-aligned headers, would have fixed all three arms.
notes: All three arms converge on the same garbled cell because 'first printing that contains the month' is the natural stopping point, and the correct digit appears only from the next printing onward. This table's row-sum identity is exact (no rounding), which makes it an ideal automatic check. A two-series elasticity is highly sensitive to one digit in the small P series. Data note for whoever owns error_bins.py: the index bin is '>25pct' although Opus's own sensitivity analysis puts the relative gap between the GLM answer and Opus's answer at roughly a tenth. The bin may reflect how the reference is expressed; this was not investigated (no reference access).
